title: Possession & Relationships: Whose Is It?
description: Learn common possessive forms through source-checked examples and repeated participant tracking.

sourceReview.notes: Possessive forms and examples are taken from the modern Reference Grammar. The lesson introduces the existence of a-class/o-class relationships without pretending the distinction can be reduced to one simple English rule.

activities.instruction: Start with a familiar o-class example.
activities.prompt: Focus on whose thing is being discussed.
activities.support: The modern reference gives this exact phrase.
activities.patternIntro: koʻu marks a first-person singular o-class possessive relationship.
activities.languageNote: Do not assume every English 'my' uses koʻu; Hawaiian has both o-class and a-class possessive relationships.

activities.prompt: Now the possessor is the listener.
activities.support: This source example uses an o-class possessive.
activities.patternIntro: kou marks second-person singular possession in this sourced o-class example.
activities.languageNote: The possessor changed from speaker to listener.

activities.prompt: English still says 'your,' but Hawaiian uses a different possessive class here.
activities.support: This exact example is listed in the modern reference grammar.
activities.patternIntro: kāu is the second-person singular a-class form in this example.
activities.languageNote: Do not reduce a-class/o-class to a single memorized English rule. Learn the relationship patterns with examples.

activities.prompt: The owner/relationship is now someone else.
activities.support: This is a sourced a-class example.
activities.patternIntro: kāna is third-person singular a-class in this source example.
activities.languageNote: Third-person forms also vary by possessive class.

activities.prompt: Track both class and who the possessor group is.
activities.support: This exact source example uses a plural third-person possessor.
activities.patternIntro: lākou means they (three or more); kā lākou is the corresponding a-class possessive phrase here.
activities.languageNote: Your pronoun knowledge now helps decode possession too.

activities.support: māua still means two people including the speaker but excluding the listener.
activities.patternIntro: The possessive frame preserves the dual exclusive meaning of māua.
activities.languageNote: Possessive grammar builds on the pronoun system rather than replacing it.

activities.instruction: Find possession inside a full sentence.
activities.support: This exact source sentence places Kimo at the speaker's house.
activities.sentence: Aia ʻo Kimo ma koʻu hale.
activities.patternIntro: koʻu modifies hale while the sentence as a whole tells where Kimo is.
activities.languageNote: Understanding koʻu changes whose location is being described.

activities.prompt: Aia ʻo Kimo ma koʻu hale.
activities.explanation: koʻu means my in this sourced o-class example.

activities.support: Is the listener included in 'our' here?
activities.explanation: māua is dual exclusive, so the listener is not included.

activities.support: How many people does lākou refer to?
What is the important lesson from this contrast?
options: English 'your' can map to different Hawaiian possessive classes
kou is singular and kāu is plural
activities.answer: English 'your' can map to different Hawaiian possessive classes
activities.explanation: Hawaiian distinguishes a-class and o-class possessive relationships; English 'your' does not show that distinction.
